sentences: Revolving credit utilization is the most important driver of default risk, and risk generally increases as the share of the credit limit in use rises.
Its effect is concentrated at high levels: risk shows a sharp step up once utilization passes about 0.72.
Past delinquencies are the second or third most important driver, and having any delinquency raises the risk of default compared with having none.
Annual income is also among the leading drivers, with higher income generally lowering the risk of default.
Length of credit history has at most a weak effect, with longer histories generally associated with lower risk.
The effect of utilization grows with the number of past delinquencies, so high utilization matters more for applicants who have delinquencies.
The data do not settle whether the effect of utilization depends on credit history length.
Debt-to-income ratio hardly matters, and the data do not show a clear pattern in its effect.
Age, number of dependents, months at address and recent credit inquiries have no detectable effect on predicted default risk.
